title: Introducing Yourself
pronunciation_focus_summary: Liaison — linking the final consonant of one word to the vowel starting the next word, like 'je suis‿un' and 'c'est‿un'.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'je' is a soft 'zh' sound. The double 'l' in 'appelle' is pronounced clearly. Stress falls on the last syllable.
Notice the liaison: 'vous‿appelez' — the 's' of 'vous' links to the 'a' of 'appelez', making a 'z' sound.
Liaison between 'suis' and 'américain' — the 's' links as a 'z' sound. The nasal 'ain' at the end.
The 'j'' is an elision — 'je' drops its 'e' before a vowel. This is mandatory, not optional.
phrases.example_sentence: J'habite à Paris depuis deux ans.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'ien' in 'viens' is a nasal vowel — lips spread, air through nose. Don't pronounce the final 's'.
Two nasal vowels: 'en' and 'an' — both are the same nasal sound (ɑ̃). The final 'é' is a clear 'ay' sound.
Liaison: 'quel‿âge' links smoothly. The 'â' in 'âge' is an open 'ah' sound.
phrases.example_sentence: Quel âge avez-vous, si ce n'est pas indiscret ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'e' in 'trente' is silent. Liaison: 'trente‿ans' — the 't' links to 'ans'. Two nasal sounds close together.
phrases.example_sentence: J'ai trente ans et j'habite à Lyon.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'un' is a nasal vowel (lips rounded). 'Peu' has the 'eu' sound — round your lips like 'oo' but say 'uh'.
phrases.example_sentence: Je parle un peu français, mais je suis encore débutant.

phrases.text: Je ne parle pas bien français
phrases.phonetic_ipa: ʒə nə paʁl pa bjɛ̃ fʁɑ̃sɛ
phrases.phonetic_approx: zhuh nuh PAHRL pah byehn frahn-SEH
phrases.pronunciation_notes: The negation 'ne...pas' wraps the verb. In casual speech, 'ne' is often dropped: 'je parle pas'.
phrases.example_sentence: Désolé, je ne parle pas bien français.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Rising intonation makes it a question. The 'ais' in 'anglais' sounds like 'eh' (open E).
Liaison: 'suis‿étudiant' — the 's' links as 'z'. The 'u' in 'étudiant' is the French U (lips rounded, tongue forward).
The 'aille' sounds like 'eye' with a y sound. The 'dans' has a nasal vowel.
The French R starts this phrase — practice the uvular sound. The 'aî' in 'connaître' is an open 'eh' sound.
phrases.example_sentence: Ravi de vous connaître, je suis Marc.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Liaison: 'c'est‿un' — the 't' links to 'un'. The nasal 'un' and the French R at the end.
phrases.example_sentence: C'est un plaisir de vous rencontrer.

dialogues.context: Meeting someone at a language exchange event

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Enchanté, Sarah ! Je m'appelle Thomas. Vous êtes américaine ?
exchanges.translation: Nice to meet you, Sarah! My name is Thomas. Are you American?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: ahn-shahn-TAY sah-RAH! zhuh mah-PEL toh-MAH. vooz ET ah-may-ree-KEN?

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Oui, je viens de New York. Et vous ?
exchanges.translation: Yes, I come from New York. And you?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: WEE, zhuh VYEHN duh New York. ay VOO?

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Je suis français, j'habite à Paris.
exchanges.translation: I'm French, I live in Paris.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: zhuh SWEE frahn-SEH, zhah-BEET ah pah-REE

dialogues.notes: Use 'vous' (formal) when meeting someone for the first time. 'Tu' is for friends and family.

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Je m'appelle Alex. Je travaille dans la finance.
exchanges.translation: My name is Alex. I work in finance.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: zhuh mah-PEL ah-LEX. zhuh trah-VYE dahn lah fee-NAHNSS

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Ravi de vous connaître ! Vous parlez très bien français.
exchanges.translation: Pleased to meet you! You speak French very well.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: rah-VEE duh voo koh-NETR! voo pahr-LAY treh byehn frahn-SEH

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Merci ! Je parle un peu français.
exchanges.translation: Thank you! I speak a little French.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: mehr-SEE! zhuh PAHRL uhn puh frahn-SEH

dialogues.notes: The French often compliment language learners. 'Je parle un peu' is a humble and appropriate response.

cultural_notes.title: Tu vs Vous — the art of formality
cultural_notes.content: French has two words for 'you': 'tu' (informal, singular) and 'vous' (formal, or plural). Use 'vous' with strangers, older people, and in professional settings. Use 'tu' with friends, family, children, and peers who invite you to. Switching from 'vous' to 'tu' (called 'tutoyer') is a social milestone — wait for the French person to suggest it.
